analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "Ross and others against Bernard and others. May it please the court, this case which is here on the certiorari to the Second Circuit involves a stockholder's derivative action. The issue is whether the petitioners are entitled to a trial by jury. The petitioners, who are the plaintiffs below, made a timely demand for a jury. A defense motion to strike the jury demand was denied by the District Court. The Second Circuit, by a two-to-one vote, reversed on the ground that there can be no right of jury trial in a stockholder's suit, and that holding presents the principal issue here. The holding below is in direct conflict with a decision of the Ninth Circuit. It is also, we believe, in conflict with an earlier decision of the Second Circuit, which has been widely followed. The facts of the case can be stated briefly. Petitioners are stockholders of the defendant Lehman Corporation, a registered investment company. They bring this action on behalf of the corporation against its directors and against its broker, the defendant Lehman Brothers. The complaint charges that the directors of the corporation, under the control of the broker, cause the corporation to pay unnecessary and excessive commissions to the broker. These improper payments, it is alleged, violated various provisions of the Investment Company Act and constituted conversion and waste of corporate assets, willful or negligent breach of fiduciary duties. Is this a federal request of jurisdiction? It is jurisdiction under the Investment Company Act, Your Honor, under Section 44. Not a diversity case. Not a diversity case. I think the statement to the contrary and the opinion below is an error. The complaint demands judgment in favor of the corporation for an accounting and for the damages of the corporation as well as the profits of the defendants. The action thus falls into the traditional pattern of a stockholders' derivative suit. The cause of action belongs to the corporation, but the corporation cannot bring suit on it because it is under the control of the wrongdoers. A stockholder is therefore permitted to bring the action on behalf of the company. In such a suit as in others, the right of jury trial rests on the Seventh Amendment to the Constitution, which declares that in suits that common law, the right of jury trial shall be preserved. Before discussing the strictly legal questions concerning the scope of the amendment, I want to say a word about the fundamental importance of the issue. From the earliest times to the present, this court has been emphatic that the right to jury trial occupies a crucial place in our legal system, so crucial the court has said, that any curtailment or seeming curtailment should be scrutinized with the utmost care. We haven't thought of an injunction suit, for example, or a mandamus as calling for a jury trial, have we? No, Your Honor. The jury trial applies to legal issues, and I propose to show that these are legal issues, and of course the statement that your court made was addressed to legal issues. Do you suggest that there are never legal issues in a suit for injunction or a suit for mandamus? Oh, no, there can be legal issues if a suit for damages comes up at the same time as a suit for an injunction, for instance. And in that case, as your court's decision in Dairy Queen against Woodhulls, the legal issues are decided first by a jury before the equitable issues go to a court. Now, it is the great virtue of the jury system to temper the technicalities of the law and the preconceptions of judges by the common sense which twelve laymen can bring to the practical problems of life. And this virtue, I believe, has a particularly appropriate place in the stockholder's action. Wasn't that also a function, wasn't it a function of equity to get away from the rigidities of rules of law? It did, Your Honor, but I think when we speak of the jury, we think more of the factual issues rather than the legal ones. I think an appraisal of the practical problems as are presented by the facts will be for the jury, and it is there that their practical sense of justice can find application. What is the real lawsuit in this case? I'm sorry, Your Honor? What is the real lawsuit? The real lawsuit? You mean the more details of the facts? Yes. One of the charges is that... What's the suit for? The suit is for damages of the corporation and for the profits of the defendants derived from the improper commission payments. I understand that's the way you get into court. But what is the case about? Recovery of what? Damage? Money damages? Money damages? There is a prayer for an accounting which I believe, as I will argue, should be ignored. But the essence is money damages. Now, small investors consider these stockholders' action as their Magna Carta. It is their main protection, often their only protection against overreaching of management. On the other hand, from other quarters, the stockholders' action is frequently attacked for its supposed abuses. Precisely because the stockholders' action is controversial, it tends to invoke preconceptions of some judges, and precisely because of that tendency I urge the court to consider whether in this particular area of the law the practical judgment of the jury's sense of justice should be allowed to play the role which the Constitution deems of such paramount importance. Now, the court below, in rejecting the jury right in stockholders' suits, simply argued that a stockholder's action is not a suit at common law within the meaning of the Seventh Amendment. Historically, the court said the stockholder's suit was a creature of equity. It had to be brought in a court of equity so that neither side had a right to jury trial. And still, according to the court below, this historical state of the law continues to date. With deference, I say that the court below misconceived the nature of the derivative suit and the impact of the federal rules on jury procedures. The stockholder's derivative action consists of two elements. One is the cause of action of the corporation. The other is the right or standing of the stockholder to assert that cause of action. Unquestionably, the second element, the stockholder's right to act for the corporation, was developed by the courts of equity and is a creature of equity. Unquestionably, the stockholder's standing as champion of the corporation's right presents, therefore, an equitable issue which must be tried by the court without the jury. But the other element of the stockholder's action, the underlying claim of the corporation, is a wholly different thing. This corporate claim need not be a creature of equity at all. It may be a legal cause of action, which, in an action by the corporation, would entitle both parties to a jury trial. Such a legal claim of the corporation, I submit, does not change its nature because it is asserted on behalf of the corporation rather than by the corporation. For instance, a corporate claim for conversion, such as is here alleged, is typically and traditionally a claim at law. In a stockholder suit, it remains what it is. It is still a claim for conversion. It is still based upon the legal tort of conversion. It remains legal in origin and nature. Such a legal claim, we submit, is trial by jury, no matter by what mechanism the machinery of litigation is set in motion. In sum, it is our contention that in a stockholder's derivative action, the equitable issues relating to the stockholder's standing are tried by the court, but the legal issues relating to the corporation's claim are to be tried by a jury. Are you speaking now of the right to recover or the amount of recovery when you speak to the jury? Both, Your Honor. If the claim is legal, of course, the underlying claim might be an equitable claim, and then both elements would be equitable and you have no right to a jury trial. But if the corporation's underlying claim is legal, then both the existence of the claim and the amount of the claim, we say, must be determined by jury. If a proper demand is made. Now, this division of the trial functions between court and jury is a direct consequence of the merger of law and equity by the federal rules as interpreted by two recent decisions of this court. I am referring to Your Honor's decisions in Dairy Queen against Wood and its predecessor, Beacon Theatres against Westover. In short, this court held that if an action involves both legal and equitable issues, then the legal issues must be decided by a jury while the equitable issues are passed on by the court. Take, for instance, the claim for trademark infringement, which was involved in the Dairy Queen case, where the plaintiff asked both for an injunction and for damages. Formally, prior to the merger of law and equity, such a suit had to be brought on the equity side of the district court and equity would dispose of the entire controversy without a jury. Including a claim for damages? The claim for damages was disposed of by virtue of the clean-up doctrine. But before the union of law and equity, this particular suit, if brought in the 1920s, would have been disposed of as a suit and equity. That's right, Your Honor. And that was the innovation that was brought about by Dairy Queen. What was the innovation? That it is now not brought in equity. It is not brought at law. It is, of course, the single form of action declared by the federal rules. And the court sitting neither as a court of equity nor as a court of law, but simply as a court. Well, I take it that before, in the 1920s, it would have been held that this claim for damages was an equitable issue for which there would be no jury trial. Well, Is that right? I don't know whether they phrased it in terms of equitable issues. Well, how would you phrase it? But, no, I think the... I mean, if it were a legal claim... In any case, there would be no jury trial. If it were a legal claim, it wouldn't make any difference whether it was 1920 or any other time there would have been a jury trial. In 1920, Your Honor, they would have tried the whole thing in equity, not because the claim for damages was not a legal claim, but because once equity took jurisdiction, it cleaned up the whole controversy. But you mean that just suspended the Seventh Amendment? I think it was a traditional view at that time that the Seventh Amendment, so long as equity jurisdiction and law jurisdiction were separate, that equity could clean up legal claims. Were there... Are there some cases where the right to jury trial was asserted in those years and the claim was denied? I will mention one specifically, Your Honor, which involved a stockholder's derivative action, where the underlying claim of the corporation was legal and the right to jury trial was asserted. I think it will be one of my primary contentions, but I think so far as a suit for injunction and damages based on trademark violations is concerned, while I'm sure that there must have been such cases, I am not presently ready to cite one. At the present time, Mr. Houdek, if a beneficiary of a trust asserts a claim against trustees for bad faith in the investments or management or payment of excessive commissions, what kind of a suit would that be? I think, Your Honor, when you are dealing with a so-called genuine trust, where there is a separation of legal title and beneficial interest, I believe that can be brought in equity, traditionally, because that comes under the traditional head of equity jurisdiction, it would be... There would be no jury trial. There would be no jury trial in that case. But I distinguish the kind of case that you have posed from one against fiduciaries who are not technically trustees. Are you saying that the stockholders are not the beneficial owners of the assets of a corporation subject only to creditors? I think they have a beneficial interest, Your Honor, but I don't think they are considered as trustees of an express trust in the sense in which I at least understood your first question. I was thinking of the technical trust created by a trust deed or by a last will, where legal title is transferred to one person and the equitable interest to another. Now, so far as the corporation and its officers are concerned, the stockholders are concerned, I want to emphasize that the directors certainly do not have legal title. Legal title may be vested in the corporation, and the stockholders have a beneficial interest in it. But the director's position is different from that of the technical trustees, in that the technical trustee has legal title, the director does not. And I think that has always been the reason why courts have refused to apply technical trust rules to directors. For instance, the statute of limitations concerning express trusts has always been quite different from the statute of limitations applicable to directors. I gather the corporation's claim derives only from Section 44, doesn't it? The jurisdiction. The jurisdiction. What about the claim? The claim, Your Honor, there is quite... Would there have been a claim in common law for this money recovery? No, Your Honor, there is quite a number of provisions of the Investment Company Act which I enumerated in our complaint. For instance, Section 37 of the Act forbids willful conversion of assets of an investment company. We claim that there was a willful conversion. Well, what I'm really trying to get at is whether the corporation's claim for money damages, would it exist independently of the Investment Act? It could also be asserted under the common law. Well, would it have to be assertable that common law in order to bring the Seventh Amendment into play? No, Your Honor. It would not? No. Any statutory violation would bring the Seventh Amendment into play? Any statutory violation, just as much as any common law violation if it creates a claim for damages. I think generally the rule has been to understand it that even if a particular type of claim did not exist in 1791, so that you cannot say whether in 1791 it was equitable or legal, you deal with that by saying how would the courts have dealt with that claim in 1791 if that type of situation had been known at the time. Have any cases in this court given this analysis? I am quite confident that, well, certainly in declaratory judgment cases this has been held to be so in Beacon Theatres against Westover. And declaratory judgments were unknown in 1791. And incidentally, also in Beacon Theatres, Your Honor, was involved a statutory claim for tribal damages under the antitrust laws and the court held that the right to jury trial was constitutional. So I believe that answers. I say now under the doctrine of the Dairy Queen case, the trial court must scrutinize each issue whether it is essentially legal or equitable. And since in Dairy Queen the damage issue was of a legal nature, it had to go to the jury as this court ruled while the equitable issues relating to the injunction were reserved for the court. Now, I submit that exactly the same principles apply to stockholders' derivative suits. Again, in former days prior to the merger of law and equity, such an action was brought on the equity side of the district court and equity disposed of the entire controversy. But again, under Dairy Queen, the trial court must now scrutinize each issue separately for its legal or equitable character. If the corporation's cause of action is essentially legal, it must be determined by the jury even though other issues such as the standing of the stockholder are equitable and are kept for the decision by the court. Now, the majority of the court below refused to apply the principle of Dairy Queen to stockholders' suits. The court below did assume although it did not expressly hold. It assumed that the underlying corporate claim is legal rather than equitable in nature and that it is this legal claim which the petitioners are seeking to enforce here. The court below held, however, that the stockholder's action brings about a change in the nature of the cause of action and converts it from illegal to an equitable claim. I must say I fail to see by what alchemy the stockholder's suit can bring about such a transformation of the claim. After all, as I have said, a corporate claim for conversion is a legal claim and if it is asserted by a stockholder for the corporation it is still based on the same legal thought of conversion. however, I need not pursue the logic of this transformation theory of the court below since this court has squarely rejected it. The case is Flightman against Wellsberg Streetlighting Company decided in 1916 Mr. Justice Holmes wrote the opinion for a unanimous court and since the case strikes me as probably decisive here I would like to dwell on it briefly. Flightman was a stockholder's derivative action for triple damages under the antitrust laws. this court noted that the cause of action belonged to the corporation and that if the suit were brought by the corporation the claim would be at law and tribal by jury. Would it not be wouldn't that same thing not be true if a broker had charged excessive commissions to a trustee and the trustee brought the suit against the broker that would be an action at law and a jury trial but you had previously indicated that if the beneficiaries of the trust brought that suit made that claim against the trustees for having paid those excessive commissions that would necessarily be a suit in equity without a jury. But your honor these are two entirely different! things which I believe cannot be compared. Well, I just want you to clear up that lack of parallelism which at least appears on the surface. I think you would have the parallelism, your honor, if your express trustee had paid excessive! commissions to a broker and if the trustee refused to bring an action against the broker, then I assume the beneficiary could bring the action so to say derivatively on behalf of the trust, and that action would be just as much triable by jury as an action brought by the trustee himself. Does your case depend upon the right of the beneficiary to sue the broker directly? Oh, no, your honor. The beneficiary sues the broker on behalf of the corporation. The beneficiary asserts the claim for the excessive commission would be property of the trust. Now, technically, title to the trust assets is vested in the trustee, and a beneficiary can assert that claim on behalf of the trust only in a, I would say, derivative action, just like a corporate derivative action. In other words, the beneficiary would sue in the right of the trustee because the trustee is derelict in his duty in asserting the claim. Have you cited us any case or do you know of any in which a beneficiary of the kind of trust we're talking about now has been able to maintain an action in his own name against the person in the posture of the broker? The beneficiary of a trust? No, Your Honor, we have not, but I could refer you to a case in which the stockholder's action was indeed compared to such an action by a beneficiary. It's Goldstein against Grosbeck in the Second Circuit. I think the late Judge Charles E. Clark said that a stockholder's derivative action is essentially the same as or similar to an action by the beneficiary of a trust because the trustee himself refuses to enforce the cause of action. The case is not cited in our brief. You referred to a case a moment ago! In the flightman case the issue before the court as the court stated it was whether the defendant's right to a jury trial should be forfeited because the complaining stockholder was unable to induce action by the corporation and instead bought the action on behalf of the corporation. Now this court held in flightman that the answer to the question was no. In other words the derivative suit did not change the nature of the cause of action that was alleged in the flightman case. cause of action remained a legal claim under the antithrust laws and the parties were entitled to jury trial. Now I say that this part of the flightman case is directly applicable here. Here as in flightman the underlying corporate cause of action is at law. Here as there the stockholder suit does not change its nature. Here as there the parties are entitled jury to jury trial. Although I take it a while ago you conceded that at the time of flightman another kind of stockholders derivative suit had been brought not involving a trouble damage claim that there would be some kinds of stockholders derivative suits in which damages could be recovered without a jury trial at the time of flightman. As you will hear now in flightman the plaintiff Right? Is that right? That is absolutely right and you will hear that in flightman the plaintiff likewise did not succeed in getting it. Of course do the antitrust laws provide for a jury trial? No your honor the Sherman Act and the Clayton Act are completely silent and I want to repeat since the court will all seem to think that the jury right under the antitrust laws is statutory. Flightman thought so too. flightman gave a hint at it but you really cannot tell for sure what the court thought but certainly in the in the Westover case in the Beacon Theaters case this court held that the right of action for travel damages is under the constitution for to a jury right to jury is under the constitution. Now I must add that flightman had another part which I think is no longer applicable. The action was decided in the days when law and equity were separate. The action had been brought on the equity side of the court and the equity court in those days could not administer a jury trial. The court was thus faced with the impasse that on the one hand the parties were entitled to a jury trial and on the other hand the court could not grant it. So the court saw no other way out but to dismiss the action in its entirety. This extreme consequence would of course no longer be applicable today. With a merger of law and equity, the same court in the same trial can now submit the legal issues to a jury while the equitable issues remain with the court. Stockholders' action can no longer be dismissed because it asserts a legal cause of action that's triable to a jury. On the contrary, the jury right which was recognized in flight one can now be given its full scope and effect. And I think that is what should be done here. There is a second issue which the respondents have raised but since my time is about to run out, I would ask the court's permission to reserve the rest for reply. Mr. Schwartz. Mr. Chief Justice, may it please the court. I think the decisive consideration in this case was well put by my brother Houdek on oral argument and in his brief. I think the controlling consideration in his words is that a stockholder's derivative suit is a creature of equity. That being so, I think it necessarily follows that there is no right to trial by jury under either the Seventh Amendment or Rule 38 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure. This court has said on a number of occasions that the controlling test under the Seventh Amendment is the test of history. Put in other words, was there a right to trial by jury in such a case at the time of the enactment of the Seventh Amendment in 1791? Or put another way, under Rule 38, was there a right to trial by jury which Rule 38, by its own terms preserved inviolate? I think the answer to that question is historically determinable and is clear. It is clear that a derivative suit is and always has been a creature of equity so that no right to trial by jury existed which the Seventh Amendment or Rule 38 could preserve. with only two exceptions that our research has led us to, De Pinto in the Ninth Circuit and the decision of the District Court Judge McLean in this case. We know of no decision in any federal court anywhere which has ever intimated that a stockholder's derivative suit was triable otherwise than to the court as an equitable claim. So far as we know in the Southern District of New York, which I believe probably tries more suits of this kind than any other federal district, no stockholder's derivative suit has ever been tried to a jury. As the authorities cited in our brief indicated, I hesitate to use the term, but the overwhelming weight of authority, indeed the unanimous weight of authority, with the exception of De Pinto and the District Court here, has been in Mr. Haldeck's words that the derivative suit is a creature of equity and therefore conferred no jury right which the Seventh Amendment could preserve. Now, as I understand my friend's argument, it is that history must be re-read or re-written because of what I submit is a misreading of this Court's opinions in Beacon and Dairy Queen. The misreading begins with the premise that a derivative suit is in essence a combination of two claims, an equitable claim against the directors of the corporation for unlawful refusal to assert a corporate claim, and secondly the claim, what is called the underlying claim on behalf of the corporation. Beginning with that premise, Petitioner analyzes Beacon in the terms that where legal and equitable issues are joined in a single lawsuit, the Court may not, by first trying the equitable issue, frustrated the adversary's right to a jury trot. That reasoning, I submit, is wholly inapplicable here. Do you think the premise is wrong? The premise? The premise, what you referred to as the premise. There are in effect two lawsuits. Yes, sir. In the stockholder's derivative suit, Your Honor, I submit there are not two lawsuits because what my friend calls the first claim, the claim predicated upon the refusal of the corporation's officers and directors to assert the corporate claim, I say, is inseparable and indivisible from the claim asserted on behalf of the corporation. Unlike the situation, for example, in Beacon, where the claim was that the defendants had threatened antitrust litigation against the plaintiffs, had threatened to sue customers, and where the plaintiff brought an action not only for a suit, for an injunction, pardon me, against such threats, but also brought a legal claim for determination under the Declaratory Judgment Act of whether the plaintiff's conduct violated the antitrust laws. Unlike that situation where it was the plaintiff's option to state those claims separately or together, in a derivative suit, they cannot be separated out. It is an essential predicate of any derivative suit. What is the object of the derivative suit? The object of the derivative suit, Mr. Justice Black, is to assert a claim ordinarily against those who control the corporation, which the corporate entity has itself refused to assert. Would that have anything to do here with a governing law when you try the case for damages? governing law in the sense of whether it's state or federal? No, it's the law that governs the trial for damages. Is that controlled at all by the law, the principles that can give a right to recover, make the corporation bring the suit? I think not, Your Honor, if I understand your question. Our position is that once the claim is acknowledged to be derivative in nature, that is, that the plaintiff purports to assert a claim which is not his own, but a claim of another, a corporation in which he claims to own stock, that that fact and that fact alone makes the action one which was cognizable, historically inequity, and only inequity. And regardless of the nature of the claim asserted on behalf of the corporation, the Seventh Amendment conferred no right, excuse me, preserved no right which existed before. law. I point also, Mr. Justice Black, to old equity rule 27. In the 1880s, this court, after Hawes against Oakland, promulgated a rule to limit what it considered to be abuses in stockholders' derivative suits. That rule appeared in the equity rules since 1881, and it's perfectly clear from that rule that stockholders' derivative suits could only be brought on the equity side of the federal district courts. That rule was lifted almost bodily into the federal rules in 1938 as rule 23. So this court itself recognized prior to 1938 that the stockholders' derivative suit was a creature of equity, could only be brought on the equitable side of the court. And what makes it that way, may it please the court, is that it was unknown to the common law, that a man could bring a claim on behalf of another, that the whole area of corporate litigation was analogized in the first instance from the law of trusts and beyond. What is the basic right of recovery on a derivative suit? What is it the man's after that files the derivative suit? Well, in this case, on the face of the complaint, the man is after money. Yes, but what is the basic claim he has? What does he have to prove? He has to establish his right to go along with a derivative suit. He has to prove in this case, Your Honor, two things. First, he has to prove a wrongful refusal by the corporation to sue. By the corporation to sue. And then he must prove, in his words, gross breach of fiduciary duty on the part of those who control the corporation with the effect that they profited unlawfully and should disgorge their profits to the corporation. That is what he must prove. Now, either one of those issues relevant in the main action that he wants to get filed for damages? I think none of them is relevant. Only one of them. Only one is relevant to the issue of whether he's entitled to a jury. And that is... I'm not talking about a jury. I'm talking about whether he's entitled to damages. Well, if he fails to prove unlawful refusal by the corporation to bring the suit, the suit terminates at that point. He must surmount that hurdle in order to stay in court. No matter whether or not... And if he's proven that. He hasn't proven anything in connection with the ultimate suit he wants to file for damages, has he? Theoretically, that's so. Well, isn't it true practically? No, sir. Why not? It's not true practically, Your Honor, because of Rule 23, which, as I said before, lifts verbatim old equity Rule 27. That rule requires that a plaintiff either allege that he has made demand upon the corporation and it has refused to accede to that demand, or it must allege an excuse for his failure to do so. If, Your Honor, will turn to the complaint in this case, which is in the appendix, he will find that in order to comply with that provision of the rule, the plaintiff alleges on page 27 of the complaint that the demand to bring suit here would be futile because the directors are the wrongdoers, because the corporation's in hostile hands, and so on. I can say from my experience that I have never seen a complaint in a derivative case which did not contain such an allegation in order to comply with rule 23, as a practical matter, that allegation which gets him into court on a derivative basis in the first place is ordinarily the crucial issue in the case on the merits as between the corporation and the individuals. So I say as a practical matter, the very issue of demand is basic to the lawsuit itself. In my jurisdiction, Mr. Justice Black, I think the ordinary action against an administrator of an estate would be to seek his removal and the appointment of a special administrator to bring the suit. You mean they couldn't proceed against him to make him file the suit? I'm not an expert in that. I doubt it very much. If I could change the analogy with your honor's approval to a trust rather than administrator. But I suspect that in my jurisdiction there could not be a derivative suit on behalf of an administrator. But I would not be positive of that answer. I suspect it could not be done. question because it seems to me that here you have a situation where a corporation, might be an administrator, might be something else, refuses to file a suit. A man wants it filed. He thinks he has a right to recover, say, for fraud or for personal injury or for a thousand different things, all the way to trial and ensure the equity. Now, if that administrator does refuse to file, do you mean that somebody does get away to file it or force him to file it, that all that would be would be an equitable case? If, your honor, if it is a violation, for instance, of the antitrust law? If such a suit were maintainable in the federal courts, that is, a suit by a beneficiary of an estate in the name of and for the benefit of an administrator against a wrongdoer, I say that that would be cognizable only on the equity side of the court, so to speak, and there would be no right to trial by jury. And it would have to be tried without a jury? Yes, sir. The tale would wag the dog. I think not, because the tale is not that an alleged beneficiary is bringing the suit. That's the essence of the claim. A claim takes on a different coloration, has a completely different posture when it is asserted by the man who owns it, by the entity who owns it, than it does when it's asserted by one who claims to be indirectly one of many hundreds of beneficiaries. I don't think it's the tale. I think it colors the whole claim, the nature of the claim, and the manner in which it should be tried, and the manner in which it should be handled as a matter of judicial administration. I don't think it's the tale. It's either separate and distinct to me. One of the issues is that a corporation won't file a suit by reason of fraud or something else. The other issue is, if the corporation does, or it had filed a suit, can it withdraw damage? It seems to me like it entirely separate and distinct.
